audio.script_en: On her way into the school library, Mina saw a notebook on the bench beside the gate. Its cover had a small painted moon but no name on the outside. Her friend Theo wanted to look through every page to find out who had written it. Mina suggested giving it to the librarian instead, because the pages might contain something the owner did not want other children to read. They carried the closed notebook to the desk and described where they had found it. Later, a child called Eli came to the library looking worried. He told the librarian that he had lost a notebook with a moon on the cover. The librarian asked him to describe another detail without opening it in front of the class. Eli said that a green ribbon was attached inside the back cover. The librarian checked that detail and returned the notebook to him. Mina did not learn what was written on the pages, but she saw Eli smile as he put the notebook in his bag. Theo realised that finding the owner did not require showing the private writing to everyone.

sentences.text_en: The museum club was making a route map for a small school exhibition.
Arun drew one detailed map showing every display, each door and the shortest paths between them.
He liked the idea that a visitor could make any choice using a single sheet.
Mila tested the draft with her younger cousin, who followed the pictures but missed the tiny arrows between rooms.
Another visitor wanted larger print and said the crowded labels were difficult to scan.
Arun offered to remove half the displays from the map, but Mila worried that this would hide choices people might want.
They discussed whether one sheet had to serve every purpose in exactly the same way.
Mila proposed a simple main route with large arrows on the front and a detailed map on the back.
Visitors could start with the main route or turn the sheet over to plan their own order.
Arun pointed out that someone who never noticed the back would still lose those choices.
They added a large note at the bottom: more routes and all displays on the other side.
During a second test, the cousin followed the main route and a different visitor used the back to find the model room first.
The larger labels took more space, so the front could show only the main stops.
The club kept that limit visible and planned another test with visitors who had not helped design either side.

objectives: Compare expressive and factual purposes, label an imagined viewpoint, and preserve both without confusing evidence.

sentences.text_en: The class was making a book about the old mango tree in the school courtyard.
One section collected observations, such as when its leaves fell and where its shade reached at lunchtime.
Another section contained imagined adventures about birds living in its branches.
For the final page, Duy wrote that the tree remembered every child who had ever sat beneath it.
He wanted a warm ending that connected the tree with the school’s history.
Mai liked the sentence but worried that placing it after the observation section would make it sound like a fact they had established.
Duy thought removing the line would make the book less inviting, while Mai did not want to reject imaginative writing.
They looked at the page order and noticed that the two sections had similar headings.
Mai suggested giving the final page a clear heading, An Imagined Voice for the Tree, and adding a short note about the two kinds of writing.
Duy kept his sentence beneath that heading and wrote that readers could imagine other voices too.
The observation pages kept their dates and descriptions of what the class had actually seen.
When another class read the draft, several children could explain which pages reported observations and which invited imagination.
One child still missed the heading, so the editors made the section break more visible.
They did not claim that a single heading would prevent every misunderstanding, but they had a clearer way to preserve both purposes.

sentences.text_en: The library committee wanted to choose between opening earlier and staying open later once a week.
A survey beside the library exit asked visitors which change they preferred.
Of the forty children who answered during lunch, thirty chose a later closing time.
The committee’s first report said that three quarters of all pupils wanted later opening hours.
Samira noticed that the survey described library visitors who were present at lunch, not every pupil in the school.
Some children attended lunchtime clubs and could not reach the survey, while others rarely used the library at all.
A second group asked twelve children waiting for the morning bus, and nine preferred an earlier opening.
That group argued that its result cancelled the first survey and proved that early opening was the right choice.
Samira disagreed: the second group also represented a particular situation, and the two groups were different sizes.
Neither survey recorded whether a child could actually visit during the proposed extra hour.
The librarian explained that only one extra hour was available, so trying both changes every week was not possible.
The committee proposed alternating an early hour and a late hour for a short trial, while recording visits and asking what prevented other children from coming.
Jon worried that a changing timetable would itself discourage people who needed a predictable routine.
They therefore planned to publish the whole trial calendar in advance and place reminders near classrooms as well as the library.
